“A dream to some… a nightmare to others!”

That line, spoken by Merlin in director John Boorman’s 1981 epic , could very well describe the filmmaker’s experience while making , the disastrous 1977 sequel to William Friedkin’s landmark horror original. Reviled by critics, laughed at by audiences, and nearly career-ending for Boorman, Exorcist II became a cautionary tale in Hollywood about the dangers of too much of a good thing. And now, a documentary about the making of the film has been released, and it’s an engrossing look at the art of filmmaking and the tension between artist and audience.

Directed by David Kittredge, Boorman and the Devil traces where John Boorman was prior to taking on Exorcist II (namely, having just suffered through another career lowpoint with the oddball sci-fi film ) before digging in on the writing, production – including an extended hiatus during which the filmmaker was gravely ill and in the hospital – and eventual release and self-destruction of the film while the Hollywood Eye of Sauron looked on. As a matter of fact, it was during that period that Boorman, who took most of the blame for the film’s reception, said in an interview, “What do you want me to do, immolate myself on Hollywood Boulevard?”

The documentary is buoyed by interviews with key players behind the film, including a reflective Boorman himself and stars Linda Blair and the late Louise Fletcher, while commentary is also offered by various crew members who worked on the picture, film critics, and filmmakers alike, the latter of which includes, kind of randomly, Joe Dante and Karyn Kusama, and less randomly, current horror icon Mike Flanagan, who's working on his own take on The Exorcist for next year, .

Boorman, who is 93 now but apparently shot his interview for Kittredge about seven years ago, is sharp and dryly funny as he looks back at the ups and downs of not just Exorcist II – which he would rather have just been called The Heretic, as he never saw the film as a sequel as much as a “riposte” to the original – but also of his life as a filmmaker. “I've often felt that I've been braver in my filmmaking, and more cowardly in my life,” he says. “Perhaps there's only so much bravery you can muster, and I've put mine into the films.”

Boorman is sharp and dryly funny as he looks back at the ups and downs of not just Exorcist II but also of his life as a filmmaker.

Certainly, his intention with – and let’s observe the master’s wishes from here on out and just call the film by the name he’d prefer – The Heretic was noble and brave. He recalls how, in the wake of his film ’s huge success, he passed on directing the original Exorcist because, after reading the book on which it was based, he determined that it was about “torturing a child.” But by the time The Heretic came about, Boorman was licking his wounds after Zardoz and trying to get the project that would eventually become Excalibur off the ground. The two-page treatment that the studio provided him had hints of a metaphysical approach to the material that intrigued the director. As he told Max von Sydow when trying to get the actor to return for the sequel, the film would be “a beautiful poetic healing film bearing the hope of spiritual regeneration.”

And so he signed on to the project. Though in doing so, as he himself admits here, Boorman miscalculated what of film this needed to be. He may have been making The Heretic, but audiences were expecting Exorcist II. And that is where things truly went wrong.

Boorman and the Devil drags just a tad in its first chunk as it recounts the story we’ve all heard before about the sunsetting of traditional Hollywood studio films and the rise of New Hollywood, plus some time spent on the state of sequels back then (they were more Beneath the Planet of the Apes than The Empire Strikes Back at that time) and Boorman’s career. Perhaps part of the problem here is that these days it’s that much harder to differentiate a feature-length documentary from, well, a YouTube essay. Kittredge steers clear of that danger in part through his use of some slick illustrations and animation which depict behind-the-scenes events, often in comic fashion. And fortunately, once the doc gets into the guts of how The Heretic was made, as told by the people who made it – and how it went horribly wrong – the agony and the ecstasy of the project comes to life.

Louise Fletcher, who passed away in 2022, is a hoot as she recounts her time on the production, having essentially replaced Ellen Burstyn (who refused to return after the difficult production of the first film) as the adult female lead, albeit in a different role. The One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest actress (though she’ll always be Kai Winn to me) regularly has a zinger ready as she reflects on her Heretic time, like when she laughs that she “would’ve been better in the first one!” Meanwhile, un-credited co-writer, second-unit director, and “creative associate” Rospo Pallenberg, who was a frequent collaborator of Boorman’s, is also present and accounted for here, even as he’s painted as something of a villain, or at the very least, an unwanted presence by Linda Blair, among others.

Full of interesting and often funny anecdotes, as well as some scary ones – too many people wound up in the hospital while making this film! – in the end, Boorman and the Devil is about the filmmaker and his own personal devil, which is figuring out how to make his art while also satisfying the masters who pay for it – not just the studio, but the audience as well. We know he found that balance eventually, but making The Heretic almost finished him off for good.

items.title: The Whisper Man Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Tragedy. Fathers desperate for connection with their sons and failing to find it. A string of murders that left a town shaken and an eerie nursery rhyme in their wake. Minds, homes, and families haunted. A cop desperate to stop the murder of a small boy before it happens. The Whisper Man has all the ingredients of a story that will chill your bones.

Based on the novel by Alex North, the film follows newly widowed crime novelist Tom Kennedy (Adam Scott), who is forced to reconcile with estranged father and retired detective Pete Willis (Robert De Niro) when his son Jake (Acston Luca Porto) goes missing. The kidnapping follows the pattern of a child abduction and murder spree that Willis solved when Tom was just a boy; the circumstances of Willis’ involvement with the crime and its perpetrator left the detective so traumatized that he ultimately abandoned his family.

The only person who might know who is behind these grisly acts — a butcher of innocents known as the Whisper Man — sits rotting in the jail cell where Willis put him. Desperate to find Jake and assigned to the case, Detective Amanda Beck (Michelle Monaghan) joins forces with Willis in a partnership that’s one of several contrivances meant to move the plot along, but said contrivances don’t always track. The circumstances surrounding the home Tom rents are so full of wild coincidences that one is left utterly baffled.

The Whisper Man draws on a hodgepodge of influences, tropes, and plotlines from past thrillers, some more successful than others. James Patterson’s serial killer novels, Slender Man, The Silence of the Lambs, The Sixth Sense, The Black Phone, and A Nightmare on Elm Street’s Freddy Krueger all shape the story; there are even shades of the Pied Piper in the mix. It’s a potentially potent mix, but as much as The Whisper Man aims to shock, the largest reveal is telegraphed fairly early on, leaving the viewer to wait for the film to catch up.

As much as The Whisper Man aims to shock, the largest reveal is telegraphed fairly early on, leaving the viewer to wait for the film to catch up. 

The base premise is inherently horrific, and director James Ashcroft (Coming Home in the Dark) delivers unsettling images and auditory motifs, but the central relationships — Tom and his father; Jake and Tom; and Willis and his nemesis, the Whisper Man — aren’t fleshed out enough to leave a deep imprint because valuable screen time that could develop those emotional stakes is instead spent on a series of side stories and characters that mostly muddle the plot.

In a world where filmmakers regularly play with and reinvent the horror genre, this one feels like it was lifted from a time capsule. Retro can have its appeal, and The Whisper Man moves along at a brisk, fairly engaging pace. But the major outcomes are foreseeable, and the surprising moments are often just bits of plotting that make no sense. The film serves up curveballs that don’t land, befuddling character choices, obvious red herrings, and one wildly disturbing villain motivation that the film absolutely doesn’t earn. While serviceably directed with some effective and entertaining moments and a remarkably stacked cast that delivers a couple of scene-chewing interactions, The Whisper Man is too full of unexplored threads and illogical turns to pay off its promise.

items.title: Strange New Worlds Recap and Review: 'And Then They Go and Die on You'
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Now that’s more like it. After the past several weeks of / Strange New Worlds episodes, the show finally gets back on track with a good old space adventure. Sure, it’s still a concept episode in its way (or two, I suppose, doing The Poseidon Adventure in space alongside an hour of Jack Bauer-style, real-time action), but it’s one that works in spades and is never overshadowed its concepts.

“Off-Hour” certainly benefits from its focus on two of the show’s best characters, Dr. M’Benga (Babs Olusanmokun) and Nurse Chapel (Jess Bush), and the relationship that has been established between the two over the course of the past three and a half seasons. But beyond that, the episode also gives us some nice Scotty (Martin Quinn)/Pelia (Carol Kane) interplay. And it’s also just a cracking good hour of drama, action, and sci-fi spectacle.

When the Enterprise gets stuck in a slipstream wormhole, the devastation wreaked on the ship is abrupt – and fatal for some. Then there’s the crewmembers like M’Benga, who survives the initial blast but is mortally wounded; the doctor specifically is trapped behind a medical bay table, which has crashed into him and essentially severed his body at the midsection. Once the table is moved, he’ll be dead. But that’s where Chapel comes in…

I just mentioned in my interview with Olusanmokun a couple of weeks ago that the thing about Dr. M’Benga is we know he’s going to survive the show, because his character shows up on The Original Series. But somehow that knowledge doesn’t take the tension out of his predicament this week, perhaps because Strange New Worlds plays so fast and loose with continuity that I was actually thinking while watching, “Maybe that’s a M’Benga on The Original Series!” But also because the relationship between M’Benga and Chapel is so well-realized that just seeing them deal with this situation, and the emotion between them, is gripping in and of itself.

It’s also magnified by the fact that we learn here that M’Benga is thinking about leaving the Enterprise, and has even called in Dr. Boyce (Brian Markinson, who has previously appeared on TNG, DS9, and Voyager!) – the former (interim) chief medical officer of the Enterprise – to presumably replace him when he leaves. This is intriguing because we at home know that Strange New Worlds only has a handful of episodes left (including the abbreviated next and final season), and so characters like M’Benga and La’an who aren’t on The Original Series are going to have to start to depart the show at some point – and will be doing so one way or another, for better or worse.

Episode writer Bill Wolkoff, director Dan Liu, and the production team manage to depict space-travel danger here in a way that we have rarely seen in the franchise, as when the gravity controls onboard begin to malfunction, crushing pianos and whatnot, or when Spock and La’an have to climb onto the exterior of the ship during a pyrotechnic neutrino storm. And Scotty learning to “feel” the Enterprise and interpret its status like some kind of starship whisperer is also a nice touch, a call back (call forward?) to the Scotty who will someday say that he could tell the speed his ship was traveling “by the feel of the deck plates.”

I’m actually surprised at how much I’ve come to enjoy this version of Scotty, even as the frequent focus on him has meant that Kane’s Pelia usually takes a back seat. But here the mentor/mentee interplay between the two really works, as we see how she is helping to mold him into the man we all know he’s becoming. That all the problems the crew are facing end with a technobabble solution was perhaps inevitable, but it doesn’t make what has come before any less exciting or moving, and if anything, “Off-Hour” is a reminder that when Strange New Worlds cooks, it really cooks.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

  • Of course, this isn’t the first time Star Trek has done a “disaster in space” episode. Just look at TNG’s appropriately named “Disaster” for starters.
  • Pour one out for all those poor, irradiated bastards in Engineering who didn’t make it out after the blast doors shut. Red Shirts galore!
  • Dr. Phil Boyce was the original doctor on the Enterprise, first (and only, until now) seen in the unaired pilot of The Original Series, “The Cage.” There he was played by John Hoyt and depicted as a kindly and wise friend to Jeffrey Hunter’s Captain Pike – who also had a talent for making martinis. But interestingly, by the time of the second pilot, “Where No Man Has Gone Before” (where William Shatner made his debut), neither M’Benga nor Boyce was the chief medical officer onboard. Rather, Dr. Mark Piper (Paul Fix) served in that capacity for a one-episode stint before DeForest Kelley’s Dr. Leonard McCoy finally showed up. So how this will all work out remains to be seen.
  • Again with the gore! M’Benga being cut in half I get, and the episode is pretty restrained in how it depicts it. But then they just to show us Una’s compound fracture and Chapel’s finger breaking off. How many fingers have we lost this season now?

items.title: Batman: Bad Seeds - Sunset #1 Review
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
One of the reasons I dropped out of the comic book reviewing game for so long is that I became frankly exhausted by the perpetual cycle of crossover events dominating the Big Two publishers. The Batman franchise has certainly been no stranger to those crossovers in recent years - Joker War, Knight Terrors, Gotham War - with the third storyline in particular being a frustrating mess I'd just as soon delete from my memory banks. I can't say I particularly relished the prospect of the Bat-line being overtaken by another two-month crossover, but Bad Seeds ultimately makes a decent case for itself in its opening chapter.

With Bad Seeds, DC has a couple of cards in its favor this time around. This is an event comic centered around Matt Fraction's Batman and G. Willow Wilson's Poison Ivy, two of the best ongoing books on the stands right now. It's also a story that springs pretty naturally out of the pages of the latter book. The idea being that Pamela Isley has reached the dramatic endpoint in her short tenure as mayor of Gotham City. Faced with an armed insurrection by Commissioner Vandal Savage and his officers, Ivy ushers in a contingency plan that threatens to transform the city back into a primal jungle. Naturally, the extended Bat-family has issues with that.

As mentioned, Bad Seeds is geared toward Fraction's Batman and Wilson's Poison Ivy books (though pretty much every Batman-adjacent series will be tying into the event), so it's only fitting that the two writers collaborate on this opening chapter. The duo manage to craft a largely cohesive and stylistically coherent script. By the end, we have a clear sense of the scope and stakes of this crossover. Most impressive is how efficient Bad Seeds: Sunset #1 is at establishing the massive cast of characters and their respective roles within the story. There are a lot of moving parts here, but the issue never feels overly bogged down because of it.

That being said, while Sunset #1 juggles the large ensemble cast deftly enough, it doesn't necessarily make a strong case for why readers need to branch out and follow those many tie-in books. These characters look to be playing the same part they always do in these Bat-crossovers, dealing with the general chaos unfolding across the city while Batman battles his way to the root of the conflict.

The various scenes involving Batman's friends and sidekicks are fine, but they're very much secondary to the twin core story threads involving Ivy and Batman themselves. The Ivy scenes are where much of the dramatic weight of the book stems from, as we see a woman walled in by circumstance and struggling to figure out how to outmaneuver her enemies. As for Batman, the book taps into one of the elements that has made Fraction's run such a treat - the deep compassion Bruce shows to both his enemies and the people he's sworn to protect. His run has and continues to evoke Batman: The Animated Series in that way.

Helping to maintain cohesion between Wilson and Fraction's writing is the fact that the entire issue is rendered by Giuseppe Camuncoli and Cliff Rathburn (with the former handling layouts and the latter the finished artwork). The result doesn't entirely measure up to Camuncoli's solo work, as there's a certain sinister angularity to his figures that's smoothed over by Rathburn's finishes. Still, the book is cleanly rendered and plenty dynamic, and the artists play their part in ensuring that Bad Seeds: Sunset is an approachable, entertaining gateway into a much bigger story.

items.title: Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
I tend to appreciate risky new ideas over safe sequels, so I was pretty interested to see what the Plague Tale series would be like without its signature tornadoes of man-eating rats. But while Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy makes plenty of intriguing changes, like its focus on a different protagonist and all-new cast of supporting characters, most cause it to fall short of capturing the same magic as its predecessors. This prequel story moves away from rat armies into more ancient, unexplored horrors that don’t live up to the high standards of the series, and its shift from stealthing around as a conflict-averse child to straight up knifing folks to death in melee combat never quite works when the fighting itself is too bare bones to sustain this 12-hour campaign. That said, the simple but entertaining puzzles, gorgeous environments, and tense stealth sections that eventually arrive later on are still mostly worth playing, but this side quest feels like it takes more steps backward than forwards overall.

Resonance follows the same third-person adventure playbook that you’re probably already familiar with. In the storied tradition of fellow “crevice crawlers” like Star Wars Jedi: Survivor or God of War, you’ll pass through a series of small combat arenas and puzzle rooms with a companion in tow as you banter with one another and the load-bearing story slowly unfolds. Most of this feels pretty similar to the previous Plague Tale games, with some pretty notable exceptions: Hugo and Amicia have been replaced with one of the supporting characters from A Plague Tale: Requiem, Sophia, and the stealth mechanics have mostly been swapped out for the typical third-person melee combat that’s common in these kinds of games. Unfortunately, like many of its peers, it also does that super annoying thing where characters immediately shout out the solutions to every single puzzle mere seconds after you step into a room – but thankfully there’s an option to turn that off, which I did immediately and with great prejudice.

While Resonance’s story is one of its strong suits, it’s still not quite on par with the rest of the Plague Tale series. What starts as an Uncharted-like treasure hunt devolves into a horrifying doomsday scenario that mirrors a lot of the same themes as Innocence and Requiem, but with a cast that gets significantly less care in how they are developed. It’s like they were trying to speedrun through the backstory for Sophia, who was a fairly flat character in Requiem. There, she was a generic outsider with a heart of gold who doesn’t have much of an arc, so Resonance had quite a bit of heavy lifting to do while fleshing her out. It succeeds only modestly on that front – I definitely knew her better and cared about her more after experiencing her harrowing tale firsthand, but also found myself perplexed by the fact that she still doesn’t have a real character arc, beginning and ending as the same scallywag in pursuit of treasure. That feels a little wrong with the lifetime of trauma I just piloted her through.

Instead, the ancient history you uncover actually pays off far more than Sophia’s personal journey. The bits and pieces that are revealed through flashbacks unravel the mystery of the long-dead civilization that’s at the center of her treasure hunt, and the characters, twists, and dialogue in these sequences drew me in far more than the hunt itself. By the end, it almost felt like Sophia was just a sidekick along for the ride (like she was in Requiem) rather than the focus.

The side characters have many of the same issues as Sophia, like Leni, the luck-obsessed pickpocket who tags along but never has anything interesting to say, or Faro, the captain of your pirate crew whose only likable trait is how much of a complete knucklehead he is at every leg of the journey. Despite spending a pretty good chunk of time solving puzzles and chatting with these folks, they never grew on me as much as I’d hoped, even if Faro’s hilariously terrible haircut did make me laugh every time I saw it. That really highlighted how crucially important the relationship between Hugo and Amicia has been in the other Plague Tale games, and this cast doesn’t fill the void all that effectively. They’re not bad per se, but don’t leave nearly as strong of an impression as I’ve come to expect from games that are as focused on the story as this.

The history you uncover pays off far more than Sophia’s personal journey.

The biggest difference with this prequel spinoff is that instead of creeping around armored enemies you have no chance harming, you’ll be standing your ground with a sword in hand, parrying and dodging about the battlefield and taking out enemies in simple, repetitive encounters. The shift from stealth to all-out combat isn’t the most seamless transition – not exactly bad, but consistently shallow and sometimes sloppy, with standard light and heavy attacks, a kick to break your opponent’s guard, and just a handful of bad guys with two or three different attacks to learn. So much of the time between its entertaining puzzles is spent in these claustrophobic arenas, but there’s so little depth to combat that it almost immediately felt too one-note to sustain my interest. I mostly just wanted to get these humdrum encounters done with as quickly as possible to get back to the story and puzzles that are a substantial step above.

You at least have a skill tree you’ll occasionally be able to buy a new perk in, which do things like give you a more powerful kick that knocks people back or gain temporary protection from damage after killing enemies. But these are mostly modest upgrades that help combat go by a little faster without making it any more entertaining. Hilariously, every once in a while Resonance will introduce a new mechanic to shake up the action, like glowing red attacks you can’t parry, only to then offer skill tree upgrades that make it so you can just… parry those red attacks, functionally removing that new mechanic so combat stays overly straightforward.

In between combat, you’ll have a welcome break from fighting as you solve the kinds of light-manipulating puzzles for which the series has always been known. These are easily the most enjoyable part of the adventure, though many of them are super simple light reflecting puzzles where you’re moving mirrors around to point a beam at a door. I’ve probably played about a hundred games with puzzles exactly like this, and while I don’t need Resonance to break a ton of new ground here, they do feel like a bit of a step backward compared to the clever ways the other Plague Tale games asked me to clear my path of rat hordes. That said, when the puzzles do hit, which is maybe half the time, it can be a lot of fun to snoop around old places and piece together clues from an old journal like something out of Indiana Jones.

Thankfully, these high points become more frequent later on, when the horrors of the rats are finally replaced by a new kind of danger. I won’t spoil it for you here, but certain sections return to the type of enemy you’ve no hope of facing head-on, forcing you to get creative in escaping it. You fight this new problem by, you guessed it, reflecting light into dark areas, so some of the puzzles are the same kind of unoriginal stuff you were already doing – but because the stakes are so much higher and the process of outsmarting the enemy is so much more exciting than simply opening a door, these sections immediately feel interesting and original in the way most encounters lacks for a large chunk of the story. This sort of stuff is what the Plague Tale games have always done best, and introducing a new kind of thing to be terrified of is pretty awesome, even if you do have to deal with the significantly less exciting combat encounters that continue to happen in between.

items.title: Star Wars Zero Company Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
It makes a lot of sense that Star Wars Zero Company is the result of a collaboration between developers of XCOM 2 (now at Bitreactor) and Star Wars Jedi: Survivor (at Respawn). Those two excellent games couldn't be much more different from each other, but their strengths come together here to create a great-looking, clever tactics game that also tells one of the better Star Wars stories we've seen since Rogue One. Excellent characters, writing, music, and cinematic flair give context and weight to a campaign that centers around a diverse group of mercenaries, with Force powers and lightsabers refreshingly taking a back seat to blasters and thermal detonators. And while its turn-based gameplay is instantly familiar to XCOM veterans like me, its more aggressive playstyle and flexible characters make it far more than a simple Star Wars reskin.

The opening cutscene shows the Republic and Separatist fleets blasting away in orbit as the camera zooms in to Clone Troopers fighting battle droids on the ground, but then veers off to the side to focus on a smaller scuffle. That effectively establishes that this story takes place around the periphery of the Clone Wars rather than on its front lines. Our customizable main character, Hawks, is a former military commander who suffered a defeat and went into business for himself (or herself) with a crew of misfits. (If that sounds familiar, it may be because it's also a perfect description of Malcolm Reynolds from Firefly, and Hawks' voice even takes on a slight space cowboy drawl at times – but that's only fair, given how much Mal owes to Han Solo in the first place.)

Hawks and company immediately come into conflict with a Separatist-aligned cult known as the Infinite Coil led by the enigmatic Fathom, who is bent on spreading a mind-altering plague across the galaxy with creepy bugs. While it's hinted that this disease may be Force-adjacent, it's a welcome change of pace to be up against something at least a bit more original than yet another Sith-like villain. Fortunately, Fathom is largely allowed to remain mysterious during her chilling performance, and her relationship with her henchman son prevents her from becoming a two-dimensional villain. And even though it's not playable, she eventually orchestrates a climactic space battle unlike anything we've seen in Star Wars before.

Your main crewmembers all have compelling stories to follow as well, drawing to mind comparisons to Knights of the Old Republic (even though this isn't that kind of RPG and you only rarely make dialogue decisions). What they lack in novelty, they make up for with strong writing and acting: big blue brawler Kabb fills the obligatory role of the alien who talks funny, Jae is a scion of a mining family driven from her home by Coil, Trick is a medically discharged clone with plenty of brothers to help, Cly is the Mandalorian out for revenge, Tel-Rea is an AWOL padawan investigating Coil, and Luco is a sharpshooter who hates the Republic but hates Fathom more. Each of them has their own chain of story missions to complete that include a decent number of twists and cameos from other Clone Wars-era characters.

Your main crewmembers all have compelling stories to follow.

The personalities that stand out most to me, though, are non-combatants you interact with only at your base, a docked freighter called The Den. Runa is your personnel manager/bookkeeper, and her Separatist background sets her apart from the rest of the crew, who are more aligned with the Republic. She's also the most consistently funny, thanks to her endearing vanity and high level of sass. Her banter with the young, by-the-book Republic Intelligence officer Bennic is always entertaining while you're choosing missions at the holotable display, and she makes him a more sympathetic character as his loyalties are tested by the events of the war. Special mentions for medical droid M-3VO and Neesh, an oversized Lasat arms dealer, both of whom have some good lines.

The other thing you'll do before heading into combat is run Operations, where you'll spend your limited Intel points to pick which off-screen text adventures to dispatch your team on, unlocking more missions and earning cash and loot prizes. A lot of those do feel like blindly rolling the dice because you're asked to pick which team members to send without any indication of who might be better suited for, say, extracting hostages or hacking into a Separatist facility – so when things go wrong and people get injured it feels like, well, missing a 90% shot. But I always had a few bodies to spare on my roster, so that never tripped me up. And some of these are interesting dilemmas that give you a preview breaking down which of your team will be angry if you, for example, sell someone out to a Hutt for a few extra credits.

After you pick a mission and watch the repetitive, unskippable transit cutscene (which tends to hitch on both PC and PS5 Pro) as your team hyperspace-jumps into action, the tactical combat is easy to pick up if you've played anything in the XCOM vein. But while the fundamentals of controlling your team of four, taking cover, lining up attacks, and crossing your fingers that the RNG gods rule in your favor on a percentage to hit are similar, Zero Company is a vastly different game that encourages you to dive into the fray and push the enemy around. You’ll routinely knock them into each other, off of ledges, into an ally's overwatch zone, or line them up for an area-of-effect attack. (Just remember to always have a backup plan, because you're still going to miss those 90% shots 10% of the time.)

A big part of why I felt encouraged to do that is because, even though permadeath is on by default, your troops are pretty hard to kill. A character has to be downed three times (without being healed between missions) before they're gone for good. There also aren't that many surprise attacks, because the maps are usually pretty small and there's no fog of war, meaning you'll never be ambushed by an enemy you couldn't see. On top of that, there are no lasting consequences for taking damage until someone's downed for the first time and becomes injured, so I felt safe to take troops out of cover and into the open to absorb some punishment if it gave me a clear shot or got me close enough to an extraction zone that I could make it out the next turn. Despite that arrogance, in my first 35-hour playthrough on Normal difficulty, I didn't come close to losing anybody (though I come to this with a few thousand hours of XCOM under my belt, so your mileage may vary).

Another major distinction is that it's easy to chain together actions and give your operators more moves in a turn than their default three action points would normally allow. Advantage points are built up every time you damage an enemy (or use some specific abilities), and then you can spend them on extra abilities from any character, such as Trick's rocket launcher or Hawks' ability to grant an extra action point to a squad member. There are plenty of these, and that gives you a great reason to equip at least some people with blaster pistols: they're lower damage and shorter range than rifles, repeaters, or sniper rifles, but they can fire off three (or more) shots per turn to rack up Advantage quickly.

One of the trickier systems to master is the Backup ability that randomly rotates around your squad every turn. The character who has it can designate a teammate within range to assist them, and on their next attack that teammate will take a followup shot that always hits, even if the first shot misses wildly. It's incredibly valuable to have an opportunity to score guaranteed damage on every turn. But you have to be thoughtful about this because it's easy to waste if your backup guy doesn't actually have line of sight on the enemy, or if you land a critical hit and end up killing your target solo.

As much fun as it is to mow down dozens of hapless battle droids and watch them satisfyingly fall to pieces, Zero Company could have done with a bit more enemy variety. To be fair, there are quite a few types, including Coil soldiers who make you consider who's closest when one of them dies because their allies may absorb some of their power. There are melee guys, sniper guys, and everything in between, but pretty much the only non-humanoids you encounter are the rolling, shielded Droidekas. Those are memorable fights, but after a while everything else starts to blend together a bit even if you do have to adapt your tactics.

I saw a fair number of graphical bugs, but nothing that noticeably messed me up.

Many of the story missions stand out at least, partly because they'll do things like force you to move ahead by blowing up the area behind you or have you hold two locations at once and then extract while enemies constantly spawn in. For some of those you'll do a string of battles in a single location, and Zero Company has a cool trick to tie them together: the camera zooms in to third person and you run from one to the next, controlling Hawks directly until you walk into the combat zone. It gives you a much better sense that you're fighting in a real place than in the side missions where, more often than not, you're dropped directly and jarringly into a battle. I do wish there were more to do from that perspective than walk up to a person or thing and push a button to trigger some dialogue, because the levels you walk through look great.

That said, you'll probably see a fair number of graphical bugs during missions, particularly when enemies are air-dropped in, and the camera can get a bit wonky when it zooms in for what's supposed to be a flashy animation and shows you a close-up of a wall instead. A few times after a slow-motion overwatch reaction shot, I thought I might have to force-quit because everything hung for a good 20 seconds before resuming. But I haven't seen anything that noticeably messed me up – I never once had to reload a mission because I felt something hadn't gone according to plan thanks to a glitch. So it's safe to say that Zero Company is substantially less buggy than XCOM 2 when it first came out (and maybe even today).

Character progression is a little strange in that you're given almost complete freedom to remake most of your team at will. Hawks, for instance, can be changed from a Medic one mission to a Sniper the next, and any of the other six specialities after that. You can respec all his skill points and swap his gun out (in a wonderfully nerdy touch, each of the four weapon types has multiple different looks to pick from with their own sound effects) to further customize how you want them to play. The same goes for a lot of minor recruitable characters – excluding the incredibly handy astromech droids, which are purpose-built for handing out action points to teammates and lobbing grenades and healing items like crazy. That level of flexibility certainly encourages experimentation, even if it does make your choices matter a bit less when it comes to building out your team in the long term.

The only real restrictions are on your main crewmates, who can still be respecced but each have a defining class and a unique ability that give you a reason to keep them alive (on top of being able to complete their story missions). Jae's Last Shot triggers a fantastically helpful execution when an enemy's HP falls below a certain threshold, Kabb's melee attack refunds your action points if it kills the target, Cly has a Mandalorian jetpack that sets people on fire as she lands, Trick can resurrect himself once per mission, etc. Tel-Rea, naturally, has her own unique Jedi skill system.

One thing that can't be redone at will is the bond bonuses. When two teammates care about each other very much, they level up their bond and you get to choose between three randomly selected bonuses that apply to both of them, such as increasing ranged damage by one or going a bit farther on their first move. These are pretty small boosts on their own, but they add up over time and will significantly increase some crucial stats if you're consistent with your choices.

Things get doubly complex when you unlock the ability to give each character a secondary class, which lets you split their skill points between two class trees or concentrate on one. That opens up a whole new layer of opportunity for synergizing abilities, weapon mods, and utility items. I feel like I only scratched the surface of this potential on my first playthrough, and I've already started another on Hard to see how much I'll need to fine-tune my builds to survive.

I'm a few hours into that run, and I can already feel that the replayability of Zero Company is a bit limited relative to XCOM 2 because it's more story-focused and lacks the procedurally generated maps and randomized upgrade unlocks that make that game so dynamic. That's a sky-high bar to meet, though, so I'm not holding that against it – and I definitely missed some missions that can expire before you're able to get to them on my first playthrough, so I expect there will be a fair amount of new things to do this time.

items.title: Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
A gangland action saga spread across five decades, Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups runs 194 minutes but plays like a trailer for something else. While it’s technically a complete story — a rarity in the modern South Indian blockbuster landscape, where every other major release is actually a “Part 1” — the film is edited with the kind of snappy impressionism that becomes completely disorienting when you need to make sense of who’s who, or quite simply who’s standing where. Granted, the presence of bearded A-lister Yash of the KGF duology (often credited as “Rocking Star” Yash) goes a long way toward making it tolerable at times. The actor has layered charisma and explosiveness in his dual roles as ruthless mafioso Raya, and eventually his spurned son Rumi or “Ticket,” who seeks revenge for his abandonment. However, making sense of Toxic visually and narratively is a major challenge.

On the plus side, Toxic has a visual splendor given its period setting. The story runs from the 1920s all the way through India’s independence in 1947, and even goes a few decades further, tracing the changing face of the former Portuguese port of Goa as a reimagined haven for a heightened drug trade awash in slick suits, fedoras, tommy guns, and lavish speakeasies. It’s India’s western coast by way of 1920s Chicago, a fanciful façade that makes Toxic among the most expensive Indian movies ever made (certainly the most expensive one released thus far; it’s out-spent only by S.S. Rajamouli’s RRR follow-up, Varanasi, arriving in April, and the Hindu epic Ramayana: Part 1, also starring Yash and releasing in November). Alas, all this effort feels wasted on a completely unfocused movie whose soul resides in its opening and closing minutes but whose intervening three hours are a headache and a half.

Opening at a circus in medias res, Toxic finds a young boy nicknamed Ticket (his face painted like a sad clown) being handed over by his manic acrobat mother, Nadia (Kiara Advani), to his vengeful father, Raya (Yash) — the first of several characters introduced angrily chugging a bottle of booze. This angst-laden intro engenders curiosity; something painful has clearly transpired in these characters’ pasts, setting the stage for an explosive future. But the blanks are soon filled in at lightspeed. The powerplay for Goa’s drug trade, going back several decades, involved Raya’s unseen father alongside several Portuguese gangsters, each with their own family entanglements. Eventually, Raya and his steely older sister, Ganga (Nayanthara), become major players vis-à-vis a series of crisscrossing betrayals.

The film is quick to jump into its action set pieces, which feature blood and violence aplenty as well as the kind of macho heroic posing one might expect from a “pan-India” production emanating from the country’s south, but things go quickly awry. Like many films aimed at multiple markets, Toxic was shot simultaneously in multiple languages — in this case, Kannada and English. The latter version is appropriately flowery for a story touted as a violent fairy tale, but its attempts at poetic dialogue end up simply explaining the meaning and subtext behind the story at hand as characters deliver every line like it’s either a quip or a lofty proclamation. This has a numbing effect: After a while, no bit of dialogue actually stands out.

Equally anesthetic is the litany of breakneck action, which speed-ramps with reckless abandon. For the majority of its runtime, Toxic’s story is told by way of some rival faction or another opening fire on Raya’s crew as he overcomes the odds, but actually tracing who’s who — or why anyone is doing anything at all — is a fool’s errand. You could certainly turn your brain off to the movie’s flip-book unfurling, but watching Toxic might just require you to turn your off from time to time too. The sheer number of cuts with no legible point of focus or geography is disorienting to say the least.

Watching Toxic might just require you to turn your eyes off from time to time too. 

Sadly, the film’s sloppy assembly doesn’t end at its visual construction. Musically, it’s stuck in the early-to-mid aughts, drawing from the soundtracks of international blockbuster and arthouse darlings of the era — In The Mood for Love, Donnie Darko, Requiem for a Dream, even The Dark Knight — without much by way of originality or coherent sonic identity.

Ordinarily, the blame for all this would lie at the feet of the director, but in this case, it’s hard to imagine that Toxic — at least, the completed version now in cinemas — is at all the brainchild of filmmaker Geetu Mohandas. Her last film, the Malayalam-language gangster movie Moothon, masterfully disguised a queer drama steeped in intimate anguish. But even as one of the few women to helm such a major Indian release, it’s hard not to speculate about her actual influence (or lack thereof). Toxic feels like the product of a studio system bowing to tropes in the realm of hero worship and machismo, despite occasional attempts to subvert these expectations, with larger set pieces that depend entirely on misogynistic violence. It gets pretty gross on occasion, in a manner designed to satiate some kind of chauvinistic blood lust.

Yash’s Raya is defined by philandering and sexist jabs, but the gaze of Mohandas’ camera is markedly shifted from the male-centric lens of Indian mass media. Her focus during both sex and action is hairy chests and rolled-up sleeves instead of oily washboard abs, and her female characters are afforded more bodily dignity than the average heroine. However, these bare minimums don’t amount to much in a story where actually tracing the characters’ relationships is a game of Whac-a-Mole. Actresses like Nayanthara, Advani, Huma Qureshi, Tara Sutaria, and Rukmini Vasanth play women defined by their proximity to male gangsters — I’d list them all, but mapping the tree of the movie’s character dynamics would take several days — and they all eventually oscillate between stoic poise and outright yelling for minutes at a time until the drama becomes too grating to endure.

This aural unpleasantness applies to Yash as well, who consumes the lion’s share of the screen time as both the film’s mournful protagonist as well as his vindictive son. Although Ticket only appears in the final act despite the hopscotching timeline, it’s the rare role for which Yash has a thin goatee instead of a full beard, making him look practically unrecognizable (along with some digital de-aging). But is this enough to dramatically separate Ticket from his father? The answer is more complicated than “yes” or “no.” That both men harbor the same incandescent rage is part of the movie’s point about the cycles of male violence trickling through generations, and together, Yash and Mohandas manage to craft something special with these performances, even if we’re only exposed to glimmers of that brilliance thanks to the haphazard cutting.

As Raya, Yash offers hints of a hidden self-loathing beneath his violent, womanizing exterior, while as Ticket, he creates a unique physicality through a character whose swift parkour motions feel like something out of a fever dream. Amid the movie’s snowy and rainy settings, Ticket is the only human element that feels appropriately heightened beyond the expected limits of Indian action blockbusters. It might be one of Yash’s finest performances to date; unfortunately, it’s stuck in a movie where violence, although serving the thematic purpose of generational trauma, also seems to explode randomly, both from and against characters we’ve never seen before, and whose motives and place within the story are head-scratching to say the least. Ultimately, the result is a banal story that sometimes explodes with jarring noise.

items.title: The Dog Stars Review
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
Ridley Scott is hardly a novice when it comes to depicting determined men (and occasionally women) shouldering various degrees of emotional repression while doing whatever it takes to survive in hostile spaces. Really, from a career that spans nearly 50 years. More often than not, his films resonate — he’s the right to call himself an “influencer,” however ridiculous the quote. But his latest, The Dog Stars, which has seemed to catch the general public flat-footed, is a miss that’s too many steps removed from its emotional center to find any fresh truth in the crowded post-apocalyptic survival genre.

The Dog Stars, based on the 2012 Peter Heller novel, is not necessarily the tense action-thriller about a man (Jacob Elordi), his dog, and the unlikely ratio of hot people fighting to stay alive in a lawless, overgrown dystopia that the trailer makes it out to be. Instead, it’s largely a slow-moving survival story set years after a strange virus decimates society, leaving behind said hot people to grieve while a whole other subset of remaining people seemingly loses their minds, banding together to become violently deranged hordes who live to loot from those who are trying to keep a peaceful existence. Requisite lonesome acoustic guitar soundtrack straight from The Last of Us included, of course, along with a few other baffling country music needle drops.

The first 20 minutes alone are an extended side quest following Elordi’s mechanic Hig and his good boy Jasper on a supply run, loping through an abandoned Denver for Coca Cola products and medical supplies amid unquestionably gorgeous wide shots of the city. Hig flies through Rocky Mountain forests in his tiny yellow prop jet, his signature move being to kill the engine and just coast above it all with Jasper in the co-pilot seat, listening for a radio signal from a place called Grand Junction that’s rumored to harbor the last vestiges of civilization. It’s perfectly suited for IMAX, which is how I saw The Dog Stars. But these recurring vistas feel like excuses to shoot this for the premium screen experience using the nature cheat code, despite this being a film that would have otherwise crushed on streaming, where people aren’t captive audiences and might not be forced to feel too deeply or think about basic world-building questions, such as: What’s the deal with this mysterious killer flu anyway? How did those looters turn so feral? How does Hig still have a full supply of coffee beans (and does he have French Roast)?

It’s not entirely that this movie is patently uninterested in the society that came before, but it is more focused on how those who remain cope with the present, content to reminisce over their past lives in dull conversations. When Hig returns from his supply run to the homestead he shares with Josh Brolin’s hardened (and occasionally funny) ex-Marine Bangley, the two quibble over being happy with what they have and how best to lock down their property from the threat of the looters they call Reapers that need to be “dealt with like roaches.” (Bristling bros, !) Hig journeys out and finds his way to the father-daughter duo Jack (Guy Pearce, also doing an occasionally funny grumbly paranoid dad) and Cima (a perfectly serviceable Margaret Qualley). As they pull up tree stumps and sit under the stars together, Cima and Hig talk about their dead spouses. Hig flirts with her by talking about… golf. The Dog Stars script, written by Mark L. Smith, is the film’s dead weight, full of leaden dialogue that’s fine in a novel and sounds wildly contrived coming out of a real person’s mouth.

After a sleepy first hour, things pick up with coinciding standoffs of our central characters — Hig, Cima, and Jack in their neck of the woods, Bangley holding down his compound — vs. the Reapers, where we finally get a taste of the guns-blazing action promised in the trailer. In a stylish first-person sequence, Bangley, going full military ops mode, dons a night vision monocular that turns people into smearing neon green and their blood into proverbial paintball splatter. Hig and co. need to outrun a reaper pincer maneuver that ends with the first shock-laugh of the movie. These moments are, as you’d expect, exciting and well-directed, but the question of what are the intruders even doing hangs over these scenes. I don’t need every single character motivation explained — abstraction can be great! — but the lack of beyond “these are the bad guys consumed by inscrutable runes” who are depicted as whooping shirtless tattooed fiends is, speaking generously, not from this era of filmmaking. All of this does lead to a wild third-act shift that has some verve when the Hig trio reaches Grand Junction, headlined by Allison Janney doing the most capital-A acting of the whole movie in a ‘50s stewardess getup.

I can’t discuss a movie called The Dog Stars without talking more about Jasper the dog. As in any movie with a trusty companion, I brace myself for , hoping for the best yet expecting emotional terrorism. But, like every other connection in this movie, even man’s best pal is kept at a somewhat icy emotional distance. For all the jostling to reckon with the sheer amount of societal loss, it all ends up feeling like something to shrug off — even the stuff with the dog. Oh well, at least we have .

items.title: Sony PlayStation 27" Gaming Monitor Review
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
The separation between PC and console gaming is hazier than ever thanks to soaring prices, scarce hardware, and PC ports of formerly exclusive games. Go into the average PC gamer’s home and you’re likely to find at least one console, and that’s exactly the crowd that Sony hopes to appease with its new PlayStation 27” gaming monitor. Designed to match the look of your PS5 or PS5 Pro perfectly, it packages a QHD resolution with high refresh rate gameplay, auto-HDR, and a foldaway charging dock for your DualSense controllers for $349.99. If you’re a PlayStation fan, it’ll make a great addition to a desk-based gaming setup. If you don’t care about its PS5 look, however, this really isn’t the monitor you’re looking for.

It only takes a second to see who the monitor is aimed at. Between the black stand and white back of the monitor itself, it’s a perfect match for the PS5. The branding is minimal: a simple PS logo that peeks out above the stand when viewed from the rear.

The monitor comes perilously close to looking boring from the front. It’s the usual profile we’ve seen on flat panel gaming displays for years, with vanishingly thin bezels that lend the display a feeling of spaciousness. There are no visible controls. Toggling settings in the OSD is done with a joystick in the back. In short: black rectangle.

That is, until you start using the display’s biggest console-specific feature: its DualSense charging hook. Centered behind the display is a flip-down charging dock to store and charge your DualSense and DualSense Edge controllers when not in use. It sounds small — it small — but it’s exactly the kind of quality-of-life feature that PS5 players will appreciate. No more loose controllers or wires to clutter up your desk, just your neatly glowing DualSense under your now very PlayStation-looking monitor.

As the first real PlayStation-branded monitor (Sony Inzone also offers PC gaming monitors but is a separate line from PlayStation), I expected Sony to go big: OLED, high refresh rate, high peak brightness, and an even higher price. Instead, it went the opposite direction by offering something entirely more accessible to the average person.

Coming in at $350, it offers some pretty decent specs no matter which platform you choose. Within its slim frame, it features an IPS panel with a sharp 2560x1440 resolution. It’s built for everything from turn-based RPGs to twitch shooters, sporting a quick 240Hz refresh rate on PC and 120Hz on console (the PlayStation 5’s peak output). It also comes with Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) support so your gameplay stays fluid. It’s technically AMD FreeSync, but worked well with Nvidia G-Sync too.

While it’s not OLED, its Fast IPS panel is a good example of why you should still be paying attention to this tech. The colors are vibrant and the viewing angles are wide. It features a 1ms gray-to-gray response time which won’t get you the exceptional motion clarity of OLED but is effective at keeping ghosting away. Sony also did a good job calibrating the display from the factory. Out of the box, I measured color accuracy to be just under the industry standard of Delta E < 2, so you could even use it for image or video editing.

Around the back, the monitor’s I/O is neatly tucked away. It comes with two HDMI 2.1 ports and a DisplayPort 1.4, and a couple of USB Type-A ports and one Type-C to support peripherals and accessories. The charging hook folds away just below this, so if you tend to keep your monitor low, you may need to raise it when the hook is in use.

The stand is disappointing for the price. It’s a flat metal slab and a vertical metal tube and that’s about it. You’re able to make the usual tilt and height adjustments and rotate it but you can’t pivot into a portrait orientation. It does support standard VESA 100x100 mounts, so finding a replacement isn’t difficult if it bothers you.

The monitor has a few other PlayStation-specific tricks up its sleeve, like Auto HDR Tone Mapping which automatically adjusts the console’s HDR settings to match on setup. Also, it has a built-in speaker so you can hear your games even if you don’t feel like plugging in a headset. That shouldn’t be novel, but it’s not a given anymore. Without the connection to PlayStation, it’s not a display that would have more than a headphone jack in most cases.

But you should still use a headset. While it’s admirable that Sony included a speaker here, it feels like a “break glass in case of emergency” kind of addition instead of something I would actually recommend you use. The sound is thin and tinny, and I found it harsh to listen to for very long. It will work in a pinch, but even a cheap gaming headset will perform leagues better.

Though the PlayStation 27" gaming monitor doesn't feel cheap necessarily, there is a sense that Sony pared things back to make it as affordable as it is. The cheap stand is one example, but it shows through in other ways too.

The OSD, for example, is basic and feels too generic for a monitor like this. It's functional, but it doesn't carry the same premium touch as the hardware around it. There are a couple of neat things you can do, like displaying your frame rate in the corner or automatically changing color profiles to match the genre of the game you're playing, but beyond that, it's standard fare: brightness, contrast, saturation, sharpness, inputs and outputs, volume, and so on. It gets the job done, but it won't wow anyone navigating through the menus. Unlike the Inzone monitors, there’s also no software to allow you to make adjustments with a mouse and keyboard.

Another is the same IPS panel I was praising earlier. While those pros are definitely there, there are some cons to be aware of too. There’s nothing special about this monitor’s contrast. It’s edge-lit, no full array local dimming, so blacks can be inconsistent across the display. No matter where you’re looking, black looks closer to dark gray and it earns its decidedly average 1000:1 contrast ratio.

Its average rated brightness, 350 nits, is decidedly middle of the road. It’s not bright enough to match the highlights and shadows of most TVs these days, but does find a balance between console and PC play. When you’re playing on your PS5, the auto HDR tone mapping allows the display to better represent highlights and shadows, offering more detail within the picture. On PC, there’s no automatic tone mapping but I did find that it was bright enough to use in a well lit room.

I was able to spend about a week with this monitor ahead of this review, and I hit it hard during that time. I set up the PS5 in one input and an RTX 5090 gaming laptop in another to see how it would handle switching between both platforms. Perhaps expectedly from a company well known for its displays, it performed well for both and a fair share of productivity in between.

While it might seem like a missed opportunity to go with QHD (1440p) resolution and not 4K, I think going QHD was the smart move. 1440p sits in a sweet spot where it looks crisp and detailed on 32” monitors or below but isn’t so demanding that you need the most expensive hardware to make the most of it. There aren’t many PCs capable of running many games at 240Hz without dramatically lowering settings — a major trade-off if you’ve already shelled out for a decent gaming PC and a new monitor. At QHD, that suddenly becomes much more attainable.

Playing on the PlayStation 5, I was impressed at how well the auto tone mapping feature worked. It's not HDR, but it’s better than SDR, and that alone is an improvement over the average gaming monitor at this price. My console had no trouble detecting the monitor and its capabilities, so enabling VRR and 120Hz only required a quick trip to the settings menu.

On PC, I felt the lack of quality HDR much more but gaming on it was still visually rich and a lot of fun. IPS colors are vivid and are perfectly capable of making games look great in SDR. VRR also worked well on both my Nvidia and AMD gaming laptops.

The charging hook also worked perfectly. It’s a simple system that allows you to quickly dock a controller without giving it much thought. Like other controller docks, it needs to work and get out of the way. This does that. Missed opportunity to give the hook a bit of accent lighting like the PS5 itself though, Sony.

Taken as a whole, the monitor delivers on its promises and does no more and no less. If you strip away all the PlayStation branding, what you’re left with is a decent monitor with a mediocre stand and cool charging hook. Plenty of monitors have USB ports and 1440p resolution. Plenty of monitors offer better brightness and better HDR with full array local dimming. Many of them cost under $350.

What the PlayStation monitor offers is a quiet guarantee that everything is going to work with a minimum of setup and fuss, especially with your PS5. It’s already going to blend in with part of your setup, and if you have your PS5 visible, you can count on them being a good looking pair.

The charging hook, as seemingly small and replaceable as it is, is probably the single most important feature for making it actually feel like a PlayStation monitor. Let’s be real here. You probably won’t be looking at the PS branded back of your monitor very often. Once you set it up with your PC, the auto tone mapping becomes something you don’t even think about shortly after. But the controller, pulsing with its little status light, is a constant reminder that you’re using a PlayStation accessory. And it’s useful to boot.
